name: Tokens and Tokenization
intent: See how text is cut into the pieces a language model reads, and why that decides its cost, its limits and some of its odd failures.
scenario: A support chatbot is billed per token. It handles common words well, but mangles part numbers and unusual names, and a long customer email uses more of the limit than anyone expected.
problem: A language model does not read letters or words. It reads a sequence of integers, each standing for one piece of text from a fixed vocabulary. How the text is cut into pieces decides how many of them a message needs, so it decides the price, how much fits in the context window, and how well the model handles rare strings. People who think in words are surprised by all three.

howItWorks.title: Start from the smallest pieces
howItWorks.text: The text is first broken into very small units, such as single characters or bytes. Unseen words can then still be written as a sequence of these units. With characters, a character never seen in training is still unknown; starting from the 256 possible byte values removes even that case, which is why many modern tokenizers start from bytes.

howItWorks.title: Count the most frequent pair
howItWorks.text: Byte-pair encoding (BPE) looks at a large body of text and counts every pair of neighbouring pieces. It was adapted from a data compression method for splitting rare words into subword units in machine translation (Sennrich, Haddow and Birch, 2016).

howItWorks.title: Merge it and repeat
howItWorks.text: The most frequent pair becomes one new piece, and the counting starts again with the new piece included. Each merge adds one entry to the vocabulary. The process stops when the vocabulary reaches the size chosen for the tokenizer.

howItWorks.title: Apply the merges to new text
howItWorks.text: To encode a message, the tokenizer breaks it into the smallest pieces and applies the learned merges in the order they were learned. Common words end up as one token. Rare words, numbers and codes fall apart into several smaller pieces.

howItWorks.title: Each token is a row in a table
howItWorks.text: The model turns every token ID into a vector by looking up a row in its embedding table. The table has one row per vocabulary entry, so a bigger vocabulary means a bigger table. From here on the model works on these vectors, not on letters.

howItWorks.title: Limits and prices count tokens
howItWorks.text: The context window, the output limit and the bill are all measured in tokens, not words. The same text can be a different number of tokens with a different tokenizer, and some languages and unusual strings usually need more tokens per word than common English words do.

pros: Unseen words are built from smaller pieces instead of failing, and a byte-level tokenizer can encode any text at all
Common words are single tokens, so ordinary text is short for the model to process
A fixed vocabulary keeps the embedding table and output layer a known size
Subword pieces let the model build meaning for words it has rarely seen
cons: Rare strings, numbers and codes split into many tokens, which costs more and is harder for the model to handle
Token counts differ between tokenizers, so prices and limits cannot be compared by looking at the headline numbers
The model never sees letters directly, so spelling and character-level tasks can be unreliable
A tokenizer is fixed when the model is trained and cannot be changed later without retraining
whenToUse: You pay per token, or you must fit text into a context window
You are debugging odd model behaviour with names, codes, numbers or other languages
You are estimating cost or latency for a new workload
whenNotToUse: Do not count words as a stand-in for tokens when a limit matters: measure tokens with the real tokenizer
Do not train your own tokenizer for a hosted model: the tokenizer must match the model that was trained with it
Do not assume an identifier or part number is read as one unit
pitfalls: Estimating tokens as words times a fixed ratio, then hitting a limit on text with many numbers or codes
Comparing the price per million tokens of two models without checking how many tokens each needs for your text
Cutting text at a fixed character count and splitting a token or a multi-byte character in the middle
Asking a model to count or reverse letters and trusting the result

roles.label: Text
roles.description: The words, numbers and codes a person typed.

roles.label: Tokenizer
roles.description: Cuts text into pieces using the merges it learned, and turns each piece into an integer ID.

roles.label: Vocabulary
roles.description: The fixed list of pieces the tokenizer knows. Its size is chosen when the tokenizer is built.

roles.label: Model
roles.description: Looks each ID up in its embedding table and works on the resulting vectors.

sources.title: Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units

quiz.question: A chatbot's bill is higher than expected for messages full of order codes such as XK-9921-B, even though the messages are short in words. What is the most likely reason?
options: Codes are sent to the model twice, once as typed and once as a hidden copy
The tokenizer rarely saw such strings, so each code splits into many small tokens
The model charges a fixed fee for every message that contains digits or dashes
Codes are longer than words, so they always take exactly one token per character
quiz.explanation: Merges are learned from frequent patterns. A code the tokenizer has rarely met is not merged into big pieces, so it falls apart into small ones and costs more tokens. Nothing is sent twice or charged as a fee, and the count is not simply one token per character.

quiz.question: A team picks the model with the lower price per million tokens, assuming it will be cheaper for the same documents. When the invoices arrive, the 'cheaper' model costs more. What did they overlook?
options: Cheaper models always use a longer context window, which raises the cost of each document
Prices are quoted per million tokens, so small documents are charged as if they were large
The price per token is secret, so the headline number cannot be relied on at all
Different tokenizers can turn the same text into different numbers of tokens, so cost must be measured on their own text
quiz.explanation: A token is defined by each model's own tokenizer. One tokenizer may need noticeably more tokens for the same documents than another, which can outweigh a lower price per token. Count the tokens of a sample of your own text with each tokenizer. The other explanations are not how pricing works.

quiz.question: A developer limits answers to 500 words, but the API limit is in tokens, and some long answers are cut off in the middle of a sentence. What is the best fix?
options: Set the limit in tokens with margin, using a token count measured on typical answers
Ask the model to count its own words before it stops writing the answer
Remove the limit, because a limit in tokens cannot be made to match words
Split each answer into pieces of 500 characters before it is sent to the user
quiz.explanation: The limit is enforced in tokens, so it should be chosen and tested in tokens. Models are not reliable at counting their own words, removing the limit loses cost control, and cutting at a fixed character count breaks sentences just as before.
